title: Amalgamation Tax Rules - Canadian SR&ED Tax Credit Glossary
description: Explore the impact of a corporate Amalgamation on unused R&ED expenditure pools and investment tax credits in our Canadian SR&ED glossary.
summary: For Canadian corporations considering an amalgamation or other change in corporate control, this entry explains the federal SR&ED rules at stake: associated CCPCs share one $6 million enhanced expenditure limit, CCPCs and ECPCs earn a 35% refundable investment tax credit, and subsection 37(6.1) and paragraph 37(1)(h) restrict carryforward of pre-acquisition SR&ED pools after an acquisition of control.

body.text: For Canadian corporations considering an amalgamation or other change in corporate control, this entry explains the federal SR&ED rules at stake: associated CCPCs share one $6 million enhanced expenditure limit, CCPCs and ECPCs earn a 35% refundable investment tax credit, and subsection 37(6.1) and paragraph 37(1)(h) restrict carryforward of pre-acquisition SR&ED pools after an acquisition of control.

Between December 2024 and November 2026, Canada enacted and proposed the most expansive structural overhaul of its research and development (R&D) tax regime in over three decades. Federally, Bill C-15 (Budget Implementation Act, 2025, No. 1), substantively enacted on February 26, 2026 and granted Royal Assent on March 26, 2026, codified sweeping enhancements to the Scientific Research and Experimental Development (SR&ED) Tax Incentive Program. For taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024, Bill C-15 doubled the annual expenditure limit for the enhanced 35% refundable Investment Tax Credit (ITC) from $3 million to $6 million (increasing the maximum annual enhanced refundable credit from $1.05 million to $2.1 million), raised prior-year taxable capital phase-out thresholds from $10 million–$50 million to $15 million–$75 million, introduced a three-year average gross revenue phase-out alternative (elective for Canadian-Controlled Private Corporations and mandatory for public corporations), and extended the 35% enhanced refundable ITC to Eligible Canadian Public Corporations (ECPCs). Concurrently, for depreciable property acquired on or after December 16, 2024 and qualifying equipment lease costs first becoming payable on or after December 16, 2024, Bill C-15 reinstated SR&ED income deduction and ITC eligibility (with capital ITCs refundable at 40%). Administratively, the CRA launched an optional Pre-Claim Approval Process on April 1, 2026 (providing upfront technical determinations within eight weeks) and published a redesigned Form T661 on May 15, 2026.

Tax auditors and corporate claimants must carefully separate enacted law from unlegislated budget proposals and divergent provincial rules. On November 5, 2026, Federal Budget 2026 (Masters of our Destiny) proposed expanding SR&ED to include downstream commercialization expenses—specifically regulatory approvals, product certifications, and intellectual property (IP) registration and maintenance costs—for taxation years beginning on or after November 5, 2026, while omitting any federal patent box. Provincially, Québec consolidated seven legacy innovation credits into the asset-independent, refundable Tax Credit for Research, Innovation and Commercialization (CRIC) (offering 30% and 20% tiers) for taxation years beginning after March 25, 2025, whereas Ontario retained its $3 million expenditure cap and dual income/capital phase-outs on the 8% Ontario Innovation Tax Credit (OITC). In direct federal funding, Bill C-69 (enacted June 20, 2024) retroactively excluded bona fide government loans from grinding down SR&ED pools after 2019, Sustainable Development Technology Canada (SDTC) wound down in 2024 into NRC IRAP Clean Technology, and the Strategic Innovation Fund transitioned into the $10 million+ Strategic Response Fund (SRF).
Executive Overview and 2024–2026 Legislative Chronology

Canada's R&D incentive architecture combines non-discretionary statutory tax entitlements under the federal Income Tax Act (R.S.C., 1985, c. 1 (5th Supp.), hereafter the "Act" or "ITA") and Part XXIX of the Income Tax Regulations (C.R.C., c. 945, hereafter "ITR") with provincial/territorial corporate income tax credits and discretionary direct funding contributions. Grant-directory analyses citing CRA 2024 administrative data report approximately $4.5 billion in federal SR&ED tax credit claims processed annually, making SR&ED the foundational pillar of private-sector innovation financing in Canada.

Because Canadian R&D tax parameters shifted across multiple fiscal instruments between mid-2024 and late 2026, verifying compliance for open corporate taxation years requires tracking six distinct statutory and administrative milestones:

items: Enactment of Bill C-69 — Government Loan Carve-Out (June 20, 2024): Bill C-69 amended the statutory definition of "government assistance" in subsection 127(9) of the Act to exclude "excluded loans"—bona fide public-sector loans carrying reasonable repayment terms—retroactively effective January 1, 2020 (for loans made after December 31, 2019). Claimants whose SR&ED expenditure pools were previously reduced by unconditionally or conditionally low-interest government loans in open taxation years may file an amended Form T661 with revised tax returns, provided no new SR&ED expenditures are added after the 18-month reporting deadline.

2024 Fall Economic Statement (December 16, 2024): The Department of Finance Canada unveiled its initial SR&ED modernization framework ($1.9 billion proposed over six years), proposing to raise the 35% enhanced expenditure limit from $3 million to $4.5 million, expand taxable capital phase-out thresholds to $15 million–$75 million, extend the enhanced 35% credit to ECPCs, and restore capital expenditure eligibility starting December 16, 2024.

Draft Legislation (August 15, 2025) and Federal Budget 2025 (November 2025): Following stakeholder consultations on technical amendments to sections 37 and 127 of the Act and Part XXIX of the Regulations released on August 15, 2025, Federal Budget 2025 superseded the interim $4.5 million proposal by increasing the enhanced annual expenditure limit directly to $6 million.

Royal Assent of Bill C-15 (March 26, 2026): Following substantive enactment on February 26, 2026, Budget Implementation Act, 2025, No. 1 received Royal Assent on March 26, 2026, enacting the $6 million limit, $15 million–$75 million taxable capital and three-year average gross revenue phase-outs, ECPC access (all effective for taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024), and restored SR&ED capital property and equipment lease rules (effective for property acquired or lease amounts first payable on or after December 16, 2024).

CRA Administrative Implementation (April–October 2026): The CRA launched the optional Pre-Claim Approval Process on April 1, 2026, issued the revised Form T661 on May 15, 2026, published the updated SR&ED Lease Expenditures Policy (June 8, 2026) and SR&ED Capital Expenditures Policy (June 29, 2026), and released the updated SR&ED Investment Tax Credit Policy on October 7, 2026.

Federal Budget 2026 — Masters of our Destiny (November 5, 2026): The federal government proposed investing $930 million over five years ($235 million ongoing annually) to bring post-R&D regulatory certifications and IP registration/maintenance expenses within SR&ED for taxation years beginning on or after November 5, 2026, pending legislative enactment.

body.text: Statutory Framework and Scientific Eligibility Criteria
Subsection 248(1) Definition of SR&ED and Eligible Support Work

Entitlement to federal SR&ED deductions under section 37 and investment tax credits under section 127 depends first on whether the work satisfies the statutory definition of "scientific research and experimental development" in subsection 248(1) of the Income Tax Act. Under subsection 248(1), SR&ED means a systematic investigation or search that is carried out in a field of science or technology by means of experiment or analysis. Qualifying core work falls into three statutory branches: basic research, undertaken for the advancement of scientific knowledge without a specific practical application in view; applied research, undertaken for the advancement of scientific knowledge with a specific practical application in view; and experimental development, undertaken for the purpose of achieving technological advancement to create new, or improve existing, materials, devices, products, or processes, including incremental improvements thereto.

In addition to those three core branches, subsection 248(1) admits support work consisting strictly of engineering, design, operations research, mathematical analysis, computer programming, data collection, testing, or psychological research, solely to the extent that such work is commensurate with the needs, and directly in support, of basic research, applied research, or experimental development undertaken in Canada by or on behalf of the claimant. Conversely, routine engineering or standard practice, routine software debugging or performance tuning, platform modernization or commercial scaling using known tools, commercial project delivery, routine quality control, market validation, and (subject to Federal Budget 2026's proposed commercialization amendments for future years) regulatory certification and patent prosecution fall outside subsection 248(1).
The Five-Criteria Judicial Test and CRA "Why and How" Methodology

Canadian courts and the CRA evaluate whether industrial R&D crosses the threshold from routine engineering into SR&ED using the five-question test established in Northwest Hydraulic Consultants Ltd. v. R. (1998), consolidated in the CRA's Guidelines on the Eligibility of Work for SR&ED Tax Incentives (updated August 13, 2021) around why the work was conducted (scientific or technological advancement sought in the face of uncertainty) and how it was executed (systematic investigation):

items: Scientific or Technological Uncertainty: Was there a scientific or technological uncertainty that could not be resolved using publicly available knowledge, standard engineering practice, or routine methodologies? Commercial, financial, or aesthetic uncertainties do not qualify; the uncertainty must be whether a technical objective can physically or computationally be achieved, or how to achieve it given fundamental technological constraints. Crucially, Canadian jurisprudence recognizes system uncertainty—arising when known components, materials, or open-source software frameworks are integrated in a way whose combined behaviour creates unpredictable systemic conflicts that standard practice cannot resolve.

Formulation of Specific Hypotheses: Did the researcher or engineering team formulate specific scientific or technological hypotheses aimed at reducing or eliminating that uncertainty? Unstructured trial-and-error adjustments without an explicit causal hypothesis do not satisfy the statutory standard.

Systematic Investigation or Search: Was the overall methodology consistent with the scientific method—proceeding from problem definition and hypothesis formulation through controlled experimentation or engineering analysis, empirical observation, and logical evaluation of results by qualified personnel?

Scientific or Technological Advancement: Was the process aimed at generating new scientific or technological knowledge that advances the claimant's underlying technology base beyond its starting baseline? Commercial success is not required: an experiment or prototype that fails for a technological reason fully qualifies if the systematic investigation yields new technological knowledge explaining why the hypothesized solution fails under real-world parameters.

Contemporaneous Documentation: Were records of the hypotheses tested and experimental results preserved as the work progressed? Under CRA policy, an "SR&ED project" is scoped at the level capturing the interrelated set of activities collectively necessary to resolve the defined technological uncertainties and achieve the attempted advancement.

body.text: Federal SR&ED Tax Rates, Thresholds, and Refundability Mechanics
Dual-Benefit Structure: Section 37 Deduction Pool and Section 127 ITCs

Any taxpayer carrying on business in Canada that performs eligible SR&ED in Canada can access two distinct, sequential federal tax incentives. First, under subsection 37(1) of the Act, allowable current expenditures (paragraph 37(1)(a)) and restored capital expenditures (paragraph 37(1)(b)) on SR&ED carried on in Canada enter an open-ended pool of deductible SR&ED expenditures. The claimant may deduct up to 100% of this pool against business income in the current taxation year—bypassing multi-year Capital Cost Allowance (CCA) depreciation schedules, though subsection 37(6) deems deducted post-December 15, 2024 SR&ED capital amounts to be CCA allowed—or elect to carry any unused pool balance forward indefinitely to shelter future taxable income. If the corporation undergoes an acquisition of control (a loss restriction event), subsection 37(6.1) and paragraph 37(1)(h) (including amended clause 37(6.1)(a)(i)(B) for restored capital property) stream and restrict the carryforward of pre-acquisition SR&ED deduction pools.

Second, under subsections 127(5), 127(9), and 127(10.1), the claimant earns an Investment Tax Credit (ITC) at either the 15% basic rate or the 35% enhanced rate (15% basic credit plus the 20% addition under subsection 127(10.1)) on its "qualified expenditures" at year-end. Unused non-refundable ITCs may be carried back up to 3 taxation years or carried forward up to 20 taxation years to offset Part I federal income tax otherwise payable, subject to acquisition-of-control streaming restrictions. Any ITC refunded in cash in a taxation year is deemed to have been applied against Part I tax otherwise payable, removing it from carryback and carryforward balances.

Taxability of SR&ED ITCs (ITA para. 12(1)(t)): A mandatory financial-modelling rule is that federal SR&ED ITCs claimed in Year 1 (whether refunded in cash or applied against Part I tax) are taxable in Year 2. Specifically, the Year 1 ITC first reduces the claimant's section 37 deductible SR&ED expenditure pool in Year 2; if the ITC exceeds the remaining section 37 pool balance—which routinely occurs when a claimant deducts its entire section 37 pool in Year 1 and also earns ITCs on the notional 55% Prescribed Proxy Amount—the excess is included directly in taxable business income in Year 2 under paragraph 12(1)(t).
Entity Eligibility: CCPCs and Eligible Canadian Public Corporations (ECPCs)

Prior to Bill C-15, only Canadian-Controlled Private Corporations (CCPCs) could access the 35% enhanced ITC rate; private corporations that became controlled de jure or de facto by non-resident investors or public corporations lost CCPC status and dropped immediately to the 15% non-refundable basic rate. For taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024, Bill C-15 preserved CCPC access while extending the 35% enhanced refundable ITC (on up to $6 million of qualified expenditures) to Eligible Canadian Public Corporations (ECPCs). Under paragraph (a) of the statutory ECPC definition enacted in Bill C-15 (or as an eligible subsidiary thereof), a corporation qualifies as an ECPC only if it satisfies four cumulative conditions throughout the taxation year:

items: It is resident in Canada (subparagraph (a)(i));

It is a public corporation under subsection 89(1), or would be a public corporation if "designated stock exchange in Canada" were read as "designated stock exchange"—thereby encompassing Canadian-resident innovators listed on foreign designated exchanges such as NASDAQ or NYSE (subparagraph (a)(ii));
It is not controlled, directly or indirectly in any manner whatever, by one or more non-resident persons (subparagraph (a)(iii)); and
It would not be controlled by a single hypothetical non-resident person if all shares owned by non-residents were aggregated in the hands of that one hypothetical person (subparagraph (a)(iv)).

body.text: Foreign-controlled Canadian subsidiaries of multinational corporations, Canadian public corporations failing the non-resident ownership tests or exceeding the $75 million revenue ceiling, and corporate partners of partnerships remain subject to the 15% non-refundable basic ITC.
Expenditure Limit Phase-Outs, Revenue Election, and Qualifying Income Limit

Under subsection 127(10.2) as amended by Bill C-15, for taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024, the maximum annual expenditure limit for the 35% enhanced ITC is $6,000,000 (doubled from $3,000,000 for taxation years beginning before December 16, 2024). Associated CCPCs must allocate and share a single $6,000,000 limit via Schedule T2SCH49, and ECPCs belonging to a consolidated group that prepares consolidated financial statements must likewise share a single $6,000,000 limit across the consolidated group.

For CCPCs, the default statutory formula phases out the $6,000,000 expenditure limit linearly when the combined taxable capital employed in Canada of the CCPC and all associated corporations in the immediately preceding taxation year lies between $15,000,000 and $75,000,000 (expanded from the pre-December 16, 2024 phase-out band of $10,000,000 to $50,000,000):

where A equals nil ($0) if prior-year associated taxable capital employed in Canada is ≤ $15,000,000, or the lesser of $60,000,000 and the excess of prior-year associated taxable capital over $15,000,000.

To prevent capital-intensive, pre-revenue life-sciences, clean-tech, and hardware startups from losing enhanced SR&ED access after raising large equity rounds, Bill C-15 introduced an alternative $15,000,000 to $75,000,000 phase-out based on three-year average annual gross revenue. For ECPCs, using three-year average annual revenue (drawn from the corporation's or consolidated group's financial statements over the three preceding fiscal years, presenting group members as a single economic entity) is mandatory. For CCPCs, the revenue-based calculation is elective (via prescribed form), summing the average annual financial-statement revenues of all corporations in the associated group over the three preceding fiscal years—regardless of whether those corporations were associated throughout the entire three-year lookback—with reasonable adjustments to eliminate intra-group sales. For example, a CCPC carrying $45,000,000 in prior-year taxable capital from venture financing alongside $2,000,000 in average annual revenue saw its enhanced limit crushed to $375,000 under pre-Bill C-15 rules ($3,000,000 × ($50M − $45M) / $40M), and capped at $3,000,000 under Bill C-15's default capital test ($6,000,000 × ($75M − $45M) / $60M); by electing the revenue method, its $2,000,000 revenue falls below the $15,000,000 floor, preserving the full $6,000,000 expenditure limit and up to $2,100,000 in refundable 35% credits.

Separately, per the CRA's updated SR&ED Investment Tax Credit Policy (October 7, 2026), whether a CCPC earns 40% cash refundability on the 15% basic ITC generated by qualified expenditures above its expenditure limit depends on whether it is a "qualifying corporation"—requiring that prior-year associated taxable income not exceed its Qualifying Income Limit, updated for taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024 to:

where A is nil if prior-year associated taxable capital is ≤ $15,000,000, or the lesser of $60,000,000 and the excess of taxable capital over $15,000,000 (replacing the $40,000,000 span above $10,000,000 applicable to taxation years beginning before December 16, 2024).
Refundability Matrix Across Claimant Categories and Asset Types

A vital technical audit check under Bill C-15 is that restored SR&ED capital expenditures are 40% refundable—not 100% refundable—even when earning the 35% enhanced ITC. Under the amended statutory definition of "refundable investment tax credit" and the CRA's October 7, 2026 policy, unclaimed 35% ITCs earned by CCPCs and ECPCs on current expenditures and the Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA) are 100% refundable in cash (35.0 cents per dollar), whereas unclaimed 35% ITCs earned on capital expenditures are 40% refundable in cash (35% × 40% = 14.0 cents per dollar immediate cash refund, leaving 21.0 cents per dollar as a non-refundable ITC available to offset Part I tax or carry back 3 / forward 20 years).

body.text: Qualifying SR&ED Expenditures (QREs) and Cost Accounting Rules
Salaries, Wages, Specified Employees, and Work Outside Canada

Under sections 5 to 8, clauses 37(8)(a)(ii)(A) and (B), subsections 37(1.4), 37(1.5), 37(9), 37(9.1), 37(9.5), and 78(4) of the Act, and the CRA's SR&ED Salary or Wages Policy, eligible SR&ED labour comprises gross employment income (generally T4 employment pay) incurred for employees directly engaged in SR&ED. For non-specified employees, bonuses, profit-based remuneration, and cash or reasonable actual-cost non-cash taxable benefits (excluding any recoverable GST/HST or PST input tax credits, which are deemed government assistance) qualify for the section 37 expenditure pool, though bonuses, profit-based pay, and taxable benefits are excluded from the salary base used to compute the 55% Prescribed Proxy Amount. Across all personnel, SR&ED salary or wages strictly exclude the employer's share of payroll benefits (employer CPP/QPP, EI, or group benefit premiums), extended vacation or sick leave, employee stock option benefits, and retiring allowances. Under subsection 78(4), any salary, wages, or other current expenditure accrued at year-end that is not paid within 180 days of the taxation year-end is disallowed in that year (deducted on Form T661 Line 528 for non-salary unpaid amounts) and becomes claimable only when paid.

Heightened statutory anti-avoidance caps apply to "specified employees"—defined as employees who are "specified shareholders" owning, directly or indirectly (aggregating shares held by non-arm's length persons), 10% or more of the issued shares of any class of the corporation or any related corporation, or employees who do not deal at arm's length with a specified shareholder (such as spouses, siblings, parents, or children). For specified employees, subsection 37(9) disallows 100% of bonuses and profit-based remuneration, subsection 37(9.1) imposes an overarching statutory cap on allowable SR&ED salary or wages (allocated among associated corporations via Form T1174), and Regulations 2900(7) and 2900(8) further restrict each specified employee's inclusion in the 55% proxy salary base to the lesser of 75% of total regular salary (reflected as the 75% ceiling in Form T661 Part 5) and 2.5 times the Year's Maximum Pensionable Earnings (YMPE).

While SR&ED must generally take place physically in Canada (including Canada's Exclusive Economic Zone) to earn ITCs, subsections 37(1.4) and 37(1.5) permit a claimant to include salaries or wages paid for SR&ED work performed physically outside Canada inside its Canadian section 37(1) pool and ITC calculation up to a limit of 10% of total eligible SR&ED salaries and wages paid for SR&ED carried on in Canada—provided the foreign work was directly undertaken by the taxpayer, related to a business of the taxpayer, and solely in support of SR&ED carried on in Canada. Any other current expenditures on SR&ED carried on outside Canada (such as foreign contractor invoices or foreign salaries exceeding the 10% cap) are deductible solely against current-year income under subsection 37(2) and earn zero SR&ED ITCs.
Overhead Accounting Election: Prescribed Proxy Method vs. Traditional Method

On each year's original Form T661 filing (Part 3, Section A), the claimant makes an irrevocable annual election between the Prescribed Proxy Method (ITA cl. 37(8)(a)(ii)(B), Line 160) and the Traditional Method (ITA cl. 37(8)(a)(ii)(A), Line 162). Electing the Prescribed Proxy Method allows the claimant to forego tracking actual incremental factory or office R&D overhead and instead calculate a notional Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA) under Regulation 2900(4) equal to 55% of its eligible Canadian SR&ED salary base (restricted to employees directly engaged in SR&ED). Entered on Form T661 Line 502, the PPA generates federal and provincial ITCs without entering the section 37 deduction pool (while underlying actual overhead remains deductible as ordinary business expenses). Conversely, electing the Traditional Method sets the PPA to zero (Lines 355 and 502 = "0") and requires itemizing actual overhead and support expenditures on Line 360 that are proven directly related and incremental ("but-for" causation) to SR&ED under Regulation 2900(2)(c), alongside directly attributable administrative salaries.

body.text: Subcontractors, Non-Arm's Length Contracts, Third-Party Payments, and Materials

Payments to arm's-length Canadian taxable suppliers for SR&ED performed in Canada on the claimant's behalf are 100% deductible in the section 37 pool, while 80% of the eligible contract payment qualifies for the 15% or 35% federal ITC under subsection 127(9) (invoices and statements of work must identify the eligible Canadian SR&ED activities, and the contractor must reduce its own SR&ED pool by the "contract payment" received so credits are never duplicated; payments to non-taxable suppliers are deducted at 80% on Line 528 and earn no ITCs). Consequential on reinstating capital property eligibility, Bill C-15 repealed subsections 37(14) and 37(15)—eliminating the post-2013 "look-through rule" that required payors to strip subcontractor capital outlays from contract payments—for property acquired or lease amounts first payable on or after December 16, 2024, while amending paragraph (b) of "contract payment" in subsection 127(9) to cover capital expenditures. Where SR&ED is subcontracted to a non-arm's length Canadian corporation, the contract payment itself earns no ITC; instead, both parties may file Form T1146 to transfer the performer's underlying qualified SR&ED expenditures (reported on Line 540 of the performer's T661) to the payor without the 20% arm's-length haircut. Payments to approved universities, colleges, research institutes, or non-profit R&D entities where the payor may exploit results without directing a bilateral service contract are claimed at 80% via Form T1263.

Under subclause 37(8)(a)(ii)(B)(V) (Proxy Method), Regulation 2900(2)(a) (Traditional Method), and the CRA's Materials for SR&ED Policy, materials purchased from Canadian or foreign suppliers qualify at 100% of cost in the taxation year they are physically consumed (destroyed or rendered virtually valueless) or transformed (incorporated into an experimental prototype or pilot production run retaining residual value) in the prosecution of SR&ED in Canada. Laboratory glassware (test tubes, pipettes, beakers, flasks), computer discs, cleaning supplies, lubricants, and general utilities (water, electricity, natural gas, unless energy itself is directly consumed as a process input) are not materials; they constitute overhead items. If transformed materials or restored SR&ED capital assets that generated an ITC are later sold or converted to commercial use, subsections 127(27) to (36) trigger SR&ED ITC recapture, adding the recaptured credit back to Part I tax payable.
Reinstated Capital Property, Equipment Leases, Software, and Cloud Costs

Bill C-15 reversed the 2014 repeal of SR&ED capital expenditures by enacting paragraph 37(1)(b), paragraph 37(8)(e), amended subsections 37(6), 37(8)(a)(ii), and 127(11.2), amended Regulation 2902(b), and new Regulation 2903, supported by the CRA's updated SR&ED Capital Expenditures Policy (June 29, 2026) and SR&ED Lease Expenditures Policy (June 8, 2026). Eligibility applies strictly to depreciable property acquired on or after December 16, 2024 (after December 15, 2024) and to qualifying equipment lease amounts that first become payable on or after December 16, 2024; property acquired before December 16, 2024 is excluded (though specialist SR&ED tax advisors note a narrow statutory timing interaction under amended subsection 127(11.2) warranting legal review where pre-December 16, 2024 acquisitions first became available for use afterward, and straddling taxation years must measure SR&ED operating-time percentages strictly over the post-December 15, 2024 period).

Under amended Regulation 2902(b), depreciable equipment—including laboratory instruments, CNC prototyping machines, robotics test rigs, custom tooling, moulds, and dedicated development computers or outright-purchased software—qualifies if, at the time of acquisition, it was intended either to be used during all or substantially all (90% or more) of its operating time over its expected useful life for SR&ED in Canada, or to have 90% or more of its value consumed in SR&ED in Canada; Regulation 2902(b) also restores ITC eligibility for first-term and second-term shared-use equipment. Land, inventory, goodwill, and buildings or leasehold interests in buildings are excluded under paragraph 37(8)(e), except for a prescribed special-purpose building satisfying Regulation 2903. On equipment leases, while one practitioner blog asserts leases were not restored when contrasting outright machine purchases against casual hourly machine rentals, primary Department of Finance explanatory notes (fin.canada.ca), CRA updates (canada.ca), and CRA's June 8, 2026 SR&ED Lease Expenditures Policy confirm that qualifying lease costs first payable on or after December 16, 2024 on eligible SR&ED equipment are restored—excluding General Purpose Office Equipment or Furniture (GPOEF) when electing the Proxy Method and excluding leases on property acquired before December 16, 2024. Fees for specialized development software and cloud computing space used directly for SR&ED experimentation are likewise recognized alongside these modernized rules, provided general office SaaS hosting is not double-counted under the 55% PPA.
Federal Budget 2026 Proposed Commercialization and IP Expansion

Tabled on November 5, 2026, Federal Budget 2026 (Masters of our Destiny) proposed expanding SR&ED to include downstream commercialization expenses incurred in taxation years beginning on or after November 5, 2026, estimating $930 million in support over five years and $235 million annually ongoing. Because these provisions remain unlegislated budget proposals as of November 2026, auditors must treat them as prospective measures pending parliamentary enactment and forthcoming CRA sector-specific administrative guidance. Under the Budget 2026 Tax Measures Supplementary Information, eligible commercialization costs encompass obtaining necessary regulatory approvals or certifications to bring an SR&ED-developed product or process to market, as well as registering and maintaining IP protection—strictly limited to patents, certificates of supplementary protection, plant breeders' rights, and copyrighted software developed in the course of an eligible SR&ED project. While official fees paid to foreign IP offices qualify, supporting professional work (such as patent application drafting) generally must be performed in Canada, enforcement and litigation costs are excluded, and recapture rules will claw back SR&ED deductions and ITCs if the underlying IP is subsequently sold. Budget 2026 remained silent on enacting a federal patent box, launching instead a Federal Intellectual Property Review (with further measures expected in spring 2027) and Patent Act reforms covering mandatory CIPO ownership-change registration and patent demand-letter standards.
Provincial and Territorial R&D Tax Credit Regimes

Under paragraph 37(1)(d) and subsection 127(18) of the federal Income Tax Act, all provincial and territorial R&D tax credits constitute "government assistance" that reduces both the federal section 37 expenditure pool (Form T661 Line 429) and federal qualified ITC expenditures (Form T661 Line 513, and Line 514 for provincial assistance on post-December 15, 2024 SR&ED capital property).
Ontario: Selective Bill C-15 Alignment and Three-Credit Cascade

Administered by the CRA via the federal T2 return, Ontario operates three corporate R&D tax credits. Crucially, Ontario did NOT match Bill C-15's $6 million expenditure limit or $15 million–$75 million phase-out thresholds. Auditors claiming Ontario equipment acquired on or after December 16, 2024 should therefore verify Schedule 566 instructions directly prior to filing.
Ontario's three credits operate in a strict statutory calculation sequence:

items: Ontario Innovation Tax Credit (OITC — T2 Schedule 566; Schedule 5, Line 468): An 8% refundable tax credit (historical 10% references are obsolete) on up to $3,000,000 of annual qualified Ontario SR&ED expenditures shared among associated corporations (maximum $240,000 credit; Ontario spending between $3 million and $6 million earns the 35% federal ITC with $0 OITC). OITC phases out linearly when prior-year associated federal taxable income lies between $500,000 and $800,000, or when prior-year associated taxable capital lies between $25,000,000 and $50,000,000.

Ontario Research and Development Tax Credit (ORDTC — T2 Schedule 508; Schedule 5, Line 416; Recapture Line 277): A 3.5% non-refundable tax credit (3-year carryback, 20-year carryforward) calculated on qualified Ontario expenditures minus the OITC, with no expenditure limit and no income or taxable capital phase-out.

Ontario Business-Research Institute Tax Credit (OBRITC — T2 Schedules 568 & 569; Schedule 5, Line 470): A 20% refundable tax credit on cash paid under eligible contracts with qualifying Ontario universities, colleges, hospital research institutes, or prescribed research entities, up to a $20,000,000 annual expenditure cap (maximum $4,000,000 credit).

body.text: Ontario Stacking Calculation: On $1,000,000 of qualified Ontario current expenditures (assuming no OBRITC), OITC is calculated first at 8% × $1,000,000 = $80,000; ORDTC is calculated second at 3.5% × ($1,000,000 − $80,000) = 3.5% × $920,000 = $32,200; and the federal 35% enhanced ITC is calculated last on the net base of ($1,000,000 − $80,000 − $32,200) = $887,800 × 35% = $310,730—totalling $422,930 (42.293% combined credit rate, of which $390,730 is immediate refundable cash). Applying this exact cascade to $1,000,000 of direct non-specified Ontario R&D salaries electing the 55% PPA ($1,550,000 initial qualified base) yields $124,000 OITC + $49,910 ORDTC (3.5% × $1,426,000) + $481,631.50 federal 35% ITC (35% × $1,376,090) = $655,541.50 (65.55% of direct payroll, including $605,631.50 or 60.56% in immediate refundable cash).
Québec: The 2025–2026 CRIC Overhaul and Complementary Regimes

Administered autonomously by Revenu Québec (with scientific R&D eligibility harmonized with federal subsection 248(1) and reviewed scientifically by the CRA), Québec replaced its fragmented R&D tax system in the March 25, 2025 provincial budget by enacting the CRIC—titled the Tax Credit for Research, Innovation and Commercialization on Gouvernement du Québec / Ministère des Finances portals and the Tax Credit for R&D and Pre-Commercialization on Revenu Québec Form RD-1029.8.CR-T (Codes 112 and 113)—effective for corporate taxation years (or partnership fiscal periods) beginning after March 25, 2025.

For taxation years beginning after March 25, 2025, the CRIC abolished seven legacy Québec tax incentives (which remain claimable strictly for taxation years or partnership fiscal periods beginning before March 26, 2025):

items: Tax credit for salaries and wages of researchers;
Tax credit for university research or research carried out by a public research centre or research consortium;
Tax credit for fees and dues paid to a research consortium;
Tax credit for private partnership pre-competitive research;
Tax credit for technological adaptation services;
Industrial design component of the design tax credits (fashion design remains eligible); and
Personal income tax holiday for foreign researchers and experts.

body.text: Under the CRIC, all qualified corporations—regardless of asset size or ownership—earn a 100% refundable tax credit equal to 30% on the first $1,000,000 of qualified Québec expenditures exceeding an annual exclusion threshold (allocated among associated corporations on Form RD-1029.8.EN-T), and 20% on all qualified expenditures exceeding that $1,000,000 tranche. The annual exclusion threshold is the greater of $50,000 or the sum of Québec's personal income tax Basic Personal Amount (BPA) ($18,571 in 2025; $18,952 in 2026) per employee, prorated by each employee's actual time spent on eligible Québec R&D and pre-commercialization activities. Qualified expenditures comprise 100% of Québec employee wages, 50% of Québec subcontractor payments, 50% of payments to eligible Québec public research centres, consortia, or universities, and 100% of capital property acquisition costs in Québec (excluding buildings, land, or rights to use them). Alongside traditional R&D, CRIC covers pre-commercialization activities conducted in conjunction with Québec R&D (reported on Form RD-1029.8.PR-T): regulatory validation/certification testing, product design (form, aesthetics, functionality, material selection), and quality control solely to implement a system required for initial certification. CRIC cannot be stacked with Québec's C3i investment credit or Large Investment Project Tax Holiday on the same asset. Downstream, Québec offers the Incentive Deduction for the Commercialization of Innovations (IDCI) IP box and transitions its 30% e-business credit (TCEB) to the AI-focused CDAEIA after December 31, 2025 (22% refundable / 8% non-refundable in 2026; 21% / 9% in 2027; 20% / 10% in 2028).

Illustrative Québec CRIC + Federal SR&ED Calculation (FY2026): For a Québec CCPC employing 5 full-time non-specified R&D engineers in Québec at $120,000 each ($600,000 salary, 100% R&D), its 2026 exclusion threshold is the greater of $50,000 or (5 × $18,952) = $94,760. Its 30% refundable CRIC on ($600,000 − $94,760 = $505,240) equals $151,572. Federally, its $600,000 salary plus $330,000 PPA (55%) = $930,000 is reduced by the $151,572 CRIC assistance (ITA s. 127(18)) to $778,428, earning a 35% refundable federal ITC of $272,449.80—delivering $424,021.80 (70.67% of direct R&D salary) in combined refundable cash.
Other Provincial and Territorial R&D Incentives

Across the remaining jurisdictions documented in CRA T2 corporate tax guides and provincial funding records—Alberta, British Columbia, Saskatchewan, Manitoba, Nova Scotia, New Brunswick, Newfoundland and Labrador, and Yukon—dedicated corporate R&D tax credits or grant-equivalents operate alongside federal SR&ED.

body.text: Direct Federal R&D Grants and Government Assistance Grinding Rules

Audit verification of Canadian R&D funding stacks in 2026 requires correcting widespread legacy references to terminated or restructured federal grant agencies. NRC IRAP (National Research Council of Canada Industrial Research Assistance Program) remains Canada's flagship non-repayable R&D grant mechanism for incorporated, for-profit SMEs (<500 full-time employees) operating across TRL 3 to TRL 7; grant-directory summaries citing the NRC 2024–25 Departmental Plan and Departmental Results Report document a $437 million annual budget funding roughly 3,100 to 3,360 firms annually, reimbursing up to 80% of eligible internal R&D salaries (plus ITA-negotiated subcontractor shares), with a $75,000 median award ($75,000–$200,000 typical first-time awards, up to $1 million–$10 million for major projects). Crucially, IRAP cannot fund work that has already commenced, requiring ITA engagement three to six months prior to project launch.

Three major institutional restructurings took effect across 2024–2026: Sustainable Development Technology Canada (SDTC) was wound down in 2024, with federal clean-tech R&D grants folded into NRC IRAP Clean Technology / Clean Tech Advisory Services (CTAS); Innovation, Science and Economic Development Canada's (ISED) Strategic Innovation Fund (SIF) was renamed the Strategic Response Fund (SRF), bolstered by $1 billion over six years in Federal Budget 2026, requiring a $10 million minimum contribution ($20 million+ typical project scale), 50%+ non-government co-funding, mandatory pre-consultation, and structured primarily as repayable contributions; and the Canada Digital Adoption Program (CDAP) wound down in 2025 without a federal replacement, while Innovative Solutions Canada (ISC) absorbed a $70 million annual reduction starting in 2025–26. Sectoral supports include Scale AI (reimbursing up to 40% of eligible AI commercialization costs, subject to intake pauses) and FedDev Ontario's Regional AI Initiative (RAII) (up to 50% of eligible AI costs from $125,000 to $5 million as an interest-free repayable contribution).

Under paragraph 37(1)(d), paragraph 12(1)(x), subsection 13(7.1) (for capital cost of depreciable property), and subsections 127(9), 127(11.1), and 127(18), non-repayable grants like NRC IRAP constitute "government assistance" that reduces eligible SR&ED expenditures dollar-for-dollar. Even after grinding, pairing up to 80% IRAP salary reimbursement with a 35% refundable SR&ED ITC on the claimant's 20% co-pay (plus unabsorbed PPA) recovers 60%+ of R&D payroll while respecting the 75% cumulative government assistance cap. Conversely, under Bill C-69 (enacted June 20, 2024, retroactive to loans made after December 31, 2019), bona fide repayable government loans with reasonable repayment terms qualify as "excluded loans" under subsection 127(9) and do NOT grind down SR&ED pools.
Governance, Pre-Claim Approval, Prescribed Forms, and the 18-Month Bar

While the Department of Finance Canada authors tax legislation, the CRA administers federal and harmonized provincial SR&ED claims. On April 1, 2026, the CRA launched the optional Pre-Claim Approval Process via My Business Account (Form T1322), enabling businesses to secure an upfront technical eligibility determination within 8 weeks—valid for up to three years—before commencing R&D work or incurring costs (claimants must still file Form T661 annually to substantiate actual expenditures). On May 15, 2026, the CRA published an updated Form T661 (accompanied by Guide T4088) adding revised line numbers, CRDC research codes, Pre-Claim Approval case fields, and post-December 15, 2024 capital property and lease lines, while enforcing strict word limits on Part 2 technical descriptions. Part 9 of Form T661 mandates complete disclosure of external claim preparers and contingency or flat fees (or certification of Lines 935, 970, and 975 if self-prepared); incomplete or inaccurate Part 9 disclosure triggers a $1,000 penalty under subsection 162(5.1) against the claimant and preparer jointly, subject to the due diligence defence in subsection 162(5.2).

Under subsection 37(11) and paragraph (m) of "investment tax credit" in subsection 127(9), the SR&ED reporting deadline is 12 months after the income tax return filing due date—which for corporations (ITA para. 150(1)(a), 6-month T2 due date) equals exactly 18 months after fiscal year-end (note Federal Budget 2026 proposes shifting individual T1 filing due dates to May 15 in future periods). Under subsection 37(12), missing the 18-month deadline permanently bars the claim: unreported work is deemed not to be SR&ED, and neither CRA officials nor Ministerial Taxpayer Relief discretion can extend it.

body.text: Case Law Precedents, CRA Audit Defence, and Tax Controversy

Canadian SR&ED audit assessments are governed by a well-settled line of Tax Court of Canada (TCC) and Federal Court of Appeal (FCA) authorities through 2025. Foundational decisions in Northwest Hydraulic Consultants Ltd. v. R. (1998, TCC—confirming system-level uncertainties qualify across four of five hydraulics projects), RIS-Christie Ltd. v. R. (1998, FCA), and National R&D Inc. (reapplied in Canafric Inc. v. The King, 2023, Docket 2018-677) establish that claimants must substantiate systematic hypothesis testing with objective experimental evidence rather than relying on commercial outcomes or patents alone, alongside procedural and penalty precedents in Abeilles Service de Conditionnement Inc. v. The Queen (2014 TCC 313) and ACSIS EHR (Electronic Health Record) Inc. (2015, FCA).

Modern Tax Court jurisprudence has sharpened audit boundaries across clean-tech, software, food manufacturing, and executive compensation. In Logix Data Products Inc. v. The Queen, 2021 TCC 36, the Tax Court denied a solar-shingle claim because the underlying knowledge resided in the public domain, no experimentation was conducted to achieve technological advancement, and records were deficient. Similarly, in 2025 TCC 183, the Tax Court rejected 13 food-processing projects (2005–2009) relying on trial-and-error batch adjustments, reconstructed narratives, and wages split evenly across batches without substantiation—though in a separate compensation ruling, the Tax Court held that where corporate documentation proves shareholder-manager wages were structured specifically to compensate SR&ED work, the CRA cannot arbitrarily dilute those wages based on uncompensated non-R&D duties. Crucially for software and AI firms, DAZZM Inc. v. The King, 2024 TCC 129 (Project 2501) held that systemic uncertainty in integrating open-source tools (React and Redux) exceeded routine debugging, mandated holistic evaluation of software R&D (contrasted with SCADACOM-5, where $1,293,692 of routine modernization/scale-up was disallowed as product development), and ruled at paragraph 119 that contemporaneous time sheets are not strictly required at law where objective technical metrics and credible witness testimony prove qualifying SR&ED work.

body.text: CRA field offices risk-assess Form T661 filings via CORTAX, AIMS, and Integras; CRA Access to Information disclosures (2013–2024) document 367 to 1,176 claims fully denied annually ($29 million to $76 million in denied expenditures per year), alongside gross negligence penalties for false statements or omissions made knowingly or under gross negligence. Because Canada has no domestic tax mediation or arbitration, contesting an adverse CRA technical or financial review proceeds sequentially:

items: Requesting administrative review under The SR&ED Review Process: A Guide for Claimants (updated in 2026 for Pre-Claim Approval files) prior to reassessment;
Serving a formal Notice of Objection within the statutory objection window (which Federal Budget 2026 proposes extending); and

Filing a Notice of Appeal to the Tax Court of Canada under either the Informal Procedure (whose monetary threshold Budget 2025 proposed raising) or General Procedure, with appellate recourse to the Federal Court of Appeal (note Ministerial relief for interest and penalties is restricted to extraordinary circumstances within a 10-year window).

body.text: 2026 Audit-Readiness Compliance Checklist

items: File optional Form T1322 Pre-Claim Approval via My Business Account before initiating high-value R&D projects to obtain an 8-week upfront CRA technical determination.

Engage an NRC IRAP Industrial Technology Advisor prior to incurring project payroll, and review all government loans since 2020 under Bill C-69 (ITA s. 127(9)) to ensure bona fide "excluded loans" are not erroneously ground against SR&ED pools.
Model the CCPC three-year average gross revenue election whenever prior-year associated taxable capital exceeds $15 million to protect the $6 million enhanced 35% expenditure limit.

Track post-December 15, 2024 capital asset acquisition dates, available-for-use dates, and ≥ 90% SR&ED operating-time logs, budgeting for 40% cash refundability on capital ITCs and Year 2 paragraph 12(1)(t) income inclusion.
Capture contemporaneous technical evidence—dated hypothesis logs, failed trial data, Git commits, ticket histories, and project time records—as the work occurs.

Separate the 6-month corporate T2 filing deadline (critical for Form T1145/T1146 agreements and 180-day unpaid remuneration tracking under ITA s. 78(4)) from the absolute 18-month Form T661 / Schedule T2SCH31 statutory bar.
